title: Persistence context
short: It is the EntityManager-managed set of tracked entities.
answer: It provides identity semantics and dirty checking for managed entities.
interview: It is the EntityManager-managed set of tracked entities.

title: Entity states
short: Entities can be transient, managed, detached or removed.
answer: Lifecycle state explains persist, merge, detach and remove behavior.
interview: Entities can be transient, managed, detached or removed.

title: persist vs merge
short: persist makes a new entity managed; merge copies state into a managed instance and returns it.
answer: merge does not simply reattach the same object.
interview: persist makes a new entity managed; merge copies state into a managed instance and returns it.

title: Lazy vs eager fetching
short: Lazy defers association loading; eager asks for earlier loading.
answer: Lazy can cause N+1/LazyInitializationException; eager can over-fetch.
interview: Lazy defers association loading; eager asks for earlier loading.

title: N+1 query problem
short: One parent query plus one query per accessed association.
answer: Fix with fetch joins, EntityGraphs, batch fetching or projections.
code: SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer
interview: One parent query plus one query per accessed association.

title: @Version optimistic locking
short: A version field detects concurrent updates.
answer: Hibernate includes the version in update conditions and increments it.
interview: A version field detects concurrent updates.

title: JPQL
short: JPQL queries entities and mapped fields rather than database tables/columns.
answer: Use native SQL when database-specific features or specialized queries are justified.
code: SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.status=:status
interview: JPQL queries entities and mapped fields rather than database tables/columns.

title: EntityGraph
short: It defines a use-case-specific fetch plan.
answer: It avoids making relationships globally eager.
interview: It defines a use-case-specific fetch plan.

title: Dirty checking
short: Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and synchronizes them during flush.
answer: Within a transaction, changing a managed entity can be enough.
interview: Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and synchronizes them during flush.

title: Spring Data JPA save()
short: save generally delegates to persist for new entities and merge for existing ones.
answer: New-state detection depends on entity metadata/state. SQL may be deferred.
interview: save generally delegates to persist for new entities and merge for existing ones.

title: flush vs commit
short: Flush synchronizes pending changes with the DB; commit finalizes the transaction.
answer: A flush can send SQL while the transaction can still roll back.
followups: Why can a constraint fail at flush?
interview: Flush synchronizes pending changes with the DB; commit finalizes the transaction.

title: Cascade types
short: Cascade propagates selected entity lifecycle operations.
answer: PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH and ALL are available. This differs from DB FK cascades.
interview: Cascade propagates selected entity lifecycle operations.

title: orphanRemoval
short: It can delete an owned child removed from a parent relationship.
answer: Use for composition-style ownership, not independent child lifecycles.
interview: It can delete an owned child removed from a parent relationship.

title: Optimize JPA-heavy endpoint
short: Measure SQL, remove N+1, paginate, use projections/fetch plans and indexes.
answer: Treat generated SQL as a first-class performance artifact.
code: SELECT new com.example.OrderSummary(o.id,o.status) FROM Order o
interview: Measure SQL, remove N+1, paginate, use projections/fetch plans and indexes.

title: LazyInitializationException
short: A lazy association was accessed after the persistence context was unavailable.
answer: Use explicit fetch plans and DTO mapping inside a clear transaction boundary.
interview: A lazy association was accessed after the persistence context was unavailable.

title: What is Hibernate?
short: Hibernate is a popular ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) framework for Java that maps Java objects to relational database tables, handling SQL generation, caching, and transaction management so developers work with objects instead of writing
answer: Hibernate is a popular ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) framework for Java that maps Java objects to relational database tables, handling SQL generation, caching, and transaction management so developers work with objects instead of writing raw JDBC/SQL for most operations. It's the most common JPA implementation.
interview: Hibernate is a popular ORM (Object-Relational Mapping) framework for Java that maps Java objects to relational database tables, handling SQL generation, caching, and transaction management so developers work with objects instead of writing raw JDBC/SQL for most operations. answer: JPA (Jakarta/Java Persistence API) is a specification — a set of interfaces and annotations (\@Entity\, \@Id\, \EntityManager\) — defining a standard way to do ORM in Java, without dictating the implementation. Hibernate, EclipseLink, and OpenJPA are concrete implementations of this spec.
interview: JPA (Jakarta/Java Persistence API) is a specification — a set of interfaces and annotations (\@Entity\, \@Id\, \EntityManager\) — defining a standard way to do ORM in Java, without dictating the implementation. answer: JPA is the specification/interface; Hibernate is one concrete implementation of it (predating JPA and later aligning with it). answer: A plain Java class annotated \@Entity\ representing a persistent domain object mapped to a database table — each instance corresponds to a row, and its fields (annotated e.g. \@Id\, \@Column\) map to columns. It requires a no-arg constructor and a primary key field.

answer: An association (e.g. a \@OneToMany\ collection) is not fetched from the database when the parent entity is loaded — it's only queried when the association is actually accessed in code. This avoids loading data that may not be needed, but risks a \LazyInitializationException\ if accessed after the persistence context/session has closed.

title: What is eager loading?
short: The associated entity/collection is fetched immediately, in the same query (or an immediate follow-up query) as the parent, regardless of whether it's actually used — simpler to reason about but can pull in far more data than needed and is
answer: The associated entity/collection is fetched immediately, in the same query (or an immediate follow-up query) as the parent, regardless of whether it's actually used — simpler to reason about but can pull in far more data than needed and is a common source of the N+1 query problem or oversized result sets.
interview: The associated entity/collection is fetched immediately, in the same query (or an immediate follow-up query) as the parent, regardless of whether it's actually used — simpler to reason about but can pull in far more data than needed and is a common source of the N+1 query problem or oversized result sets.

title: Difference between lazy and eager fetching.

answer: Lazy fetching defers loading an association until it's accessed, minimizing unnecessary queries/data but requiring an open session when accessed. Eager fetching loads it immediately alongside the owning entity, which is simpler but can hurt performance by fetching unused data. JPA defaults \@ManyToOne\/\@OneToOne\ to eager and \@OneToMany\/\@ManyToMany\ to lazy, though this is commonly overridden.

title: What is the N+1 query problem?
short: When fetching a list of N parent entities, and then lazily accessing an association on each one individually, Hibernate issues one query for the parents plus N additional queries (one per parent) to fetch each one's association — N+1 total
answer: When fetching a list of N parent entities, and then lazily accessing an association on each one individually, Hibernate issues one query for the parents plus N additional queries (one per parent) to fetch each one's association — N+1 total queries instead of one efficient join, badly hurting performance as N grows.
interview: When fetching a list of N parent entities, and then lazily accessing an association on each one individually, Hibernate issues one query for the parents plus N additional queries (one per parent) to fetch each one's association — N+1 total queries instead of one efficient join, badly hurting performance as N grows.

title: What are first-level and second-level caches?

answer: The first-level cache is the persistence context itself — scoped to a single session/transaction, always on, not shareable across sessions. The second-level cache (optional, e.g. via Ehcache or Redis) is shared across sessions/transactions at the \SessionFactory\ level, caching entities and query results across multiple requests to reduce database hits for frequently read, rarely changed data.

answer: Hibernate's mechanism for automatically detecting changes to managed entities: at flush time, it compares each managed entity's current field values against a snapshot taken when it was loaded, and generates \UPDATE\ statements only for entities/fields that actually changed — without the developer explicitly calling an update method.

title: What is cascading?
short: Cascading propagates an operation performed on a parent entity (persist, merge, remove, etc.) automatically to its associated child entities, so you don't have to manually save/delete each child, e.g. saving an \Order\ also saving its \Orde
answer: Cascading propagates an operation performed on a parent entity (persist, merge, remove, etc.) automatically to its associated child entities, so you don't have to manually save/delete each child, e.g. saving an \Order\ also saving its \OrderItem\s via \cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST\ on the association.
interview: Cascading propagates an operation performed on a parent entity (persist, merge, remove, etc.) automatically to its associated child entities, so you don't have to manually save/delete each child, e.g. saving an \Order\ also saving its \OrderItem\s via \cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST\ on the association.

title: Explain `CascadeType.ALL`.

answer: Applies every cascade operation (PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH) from parent to child — so persisting, updating, deleting, or detaching the parent automatically does the same for its associated children. title: What is orphan removal?
short: When \orphanRemoval = true\ is set on a one-to-many/one-to-one association, if a child entity is removed from the parent's collection (or the parent-child link is broken) without being explicitly deleted, Hibernate automatically deletes tha
answer: When \orphanRemoval = true\ is set on a one-to-many/one-to-one association, if a child entity is removed from the parent's collection (or the parent-child link is broken) without being explicitly deleted, Hibernate automatically deletes that now-orphaned child from the database on flush.
interview: When \orphanRemoval = true\ is set on a one-to-many/one-to-one association, if a child entity is removed from the parent's collection (or the parent-child link is broken) without being explicitly deleted, Hibernate automatically deletes that now-orphaned child from the database on flush.

answer: Used on the inverse (non-owning) side of a bidirectional association to indicate that the relationship is actually managed by a field on the other entity — it tells Hibernate not to create a separate join table/column for this side, avoiding duplicate/conflicting mapping of the same foreign key relationship.

answer: A fetch strategy telling JPA/Hibernate not to load the associated entity or collection until it's explicitly accessed in code, deferring the query rather than loading it upfront with the owning entity — the recommended default for collections and most associations to avoid over-fetching.

title: What is JPQL?
short: Java Persistence Query Language — an object-oriented query language similar to SQL but operating on entity objects and their fields/associations rather than tables and columns directly, e.g. \SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.customer.id = \:id
answer: Java Persistence Query Language — an object-oriented query language similar to SQL but operating on entity objects and their fields/associations rather than tables and columns directly, e.g. \SELECT o FROM Order o WHERE o.customer.id = \:id\. It's translated by the JPA provider into native SQL at execution time.

answer: JPQL queries entities and their properties/associations in an object-oriented, database-agnostic way, and JPA translates it to the appropriate SQL dialect. answer: A concurrency control strategy assuming conflicts are rare: each row carries a version column (\@Version\). No database locks are held while reading, giving better throughput for low-contention scenarios.

short: Rather than opening/closing a new database connection for every query (expensive — TCP handshake, auth), a connection pool maintains a set of pre-established, reusable connections. Application code borrows a connection from the pool, uses i
answer: Rather than opening/closing a new database connection for every query (expensive — TCP handshake, auth), a connection pool maintains a set of pre-established, reusable connections. Application code borrows a connection from the pool, uses it, and returns it rather than closing it, dramatically reducing per-query overhead and controlling the maximum concurrent load placed on the database.

answer: HikariCP is the high-performance JDBC connection pool that's Spring Boot's default. It's known for very low overhead (lightweight bytecode, minimal locking) compared to older pools, with tunable settings like \maximumPoolSize\, \connectionTimeout\, and \idleTimeout\ that need to be sized carefully relative to expected concurrency and the database's own connection limits.

title: What is the persistence context?
short: It is the set of managed entity instances associated with an EntityManager, providing identity, dirty checking and lifecycle management.
answer: Within a persistence context, loading the same entity identity normally returns the same managed instance. Changes to managed entities can be detected during flush. The persistence context also coordinates writes and relationship handling.
mistakes: Calling the persistence context a database cache.
Assuming it is shared across all threads.
interview: The persistence context is a transaction-scoped or extended unit of entity management. It provides identity, dirty checking and coordination of persistence operations.

title: Explain entity states in JPA.
short: An entity can be transient, managed, detached or removed.
answer: A newly created object is transient. persist makes it managed. After the persistence context ends it can become detached. remove marks a managed entity for deletion. merge copies state into a managed instance; it does not reattach the same object in-place.
code:
Order order = new Order(); // transient
em.persist(order); // managed
em.detach(order); // detached
em.remove(otherManagedOrder); // removed
followups: When does an entity become detached?
mistakes: Saying merge makes the passed object managed.
Treating removed as immediately deleted from the database.
interview: I distinguish object state from database state: transient, managed, detached and removed describe how the persistence context tracks the entity.

title: What is dirty checking?
short: Hibernate detects changes to managed entities and generates SQL during flush without requiring an explicit update call.
answer: Hibernate keeps enough state for managed entities to determine changes. If a managed Order amount changes inside a transaction, flush can generate an UPDATE. This is why unnecessary entity mutation can create unexpected writes.
mistakes: Calling repository.save for every field change.
Assuming dirty checking runs continuously against the database.
interview: Dirty checking compares managed entity state with its persistence-context snapshot and synchronizes changes during flush.

title: What is orphanRemoval?
short: orphanRemoval deletes a child entity when it is removed from the owning relationship collection or reference.
answer: It is commonly used for dependent child records whose lifecycle belongs to the parent. It is different from cascade REMOVE: orphan removal reacts when the child is orphaned from the relationship, while cascade remove propagates parent deletion.
code:
@OneToMany(mappedBy="order", cascade=CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval=true)
private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
followups: Is it appropriate for shared child entities?
mistakes: Using orphanRemoval for entities shared by multiple parents.
Assuming it is just a database foreign-key option.
interview: orphanRemoval expresses ownership: when a child is removed from the parent relationship, Hibernate can delete that child record.

title: How does optimistic locking work in JPA?
short: A version column detects concurrent updates and prevents silent lost updates.
answer: With @Version, Hibernate includes the version in the UPDATE condition and increments it on success. If another transaction has already changed the row, the update affects no row and Hibernate reports an optimistic locking failure.
followups: How should an API respond to an optimistic locking conflict?
mistakes: Saying @Version locks the row physically for the entire transaction.
Ignoring conflict handling and retry policy.
interview: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are relatively uncommon. A version check detects stale updates and lets the application return a conflict or apply a domain-specific retry strategy.

title: What is the N+1 query problem?
short: One query loads a parent list and then one additional query executes for each parent to load related data.
answer: For 100 orders, loading orders once and lazily accessing customer data can produce one query plus 100 additional queries. Fixes include fetch joins, entity graphs, batch fetching or purpose-built DTO queries, depending on the use case.
code:
@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.customer")
List<Order> findOrdersWithCustomer();
followups: Why can EAGER still produce poor SQL?
mistakes: Assuming EAGER guarantees one SQL query.
Fixing N+1 by making every relationship EAGER.
interview: N+1 is a query-pattern problem, not simply a lazy-loading problem. I choose fetching based on the use case and inspect generated SQL.

title: What is the difference between save and saveAndFlush in Spring Data JPA?
short: save participates in normal persistence-context behavior; saveAndFlush additionally triggers a flush immediately.
answer: save usually schedules the change in the persistence context and SQL may execute later at transaction flush/commit. saveAndFlush calls flush after saving, which can be useful when subsequent logic needs database synchronization, but it is not a commit.
followups: When can early flushing hurt performance?
mistakes: Using it after every save unnecessarily.
interview: saveAndFlush forces synchronization of pending persistence changes with the database, but transaction commit semantics remain separate.

title: How would you handle bulk updates in JPA?
short: Use bulk JPQL/SQL for large updates when appropriate, but understand that bulk operations bypass normal entity dirty checking and can leave the persistence context stale.
answer: A bulk update can be much faster than loading thousands of entities. After it, clear or refresh the persistence context as appropriate, and ensure transaction boundaries are correct.
followups: Why can bulk updates cause stale entities?
When would JDBC batching be better?
mistakes: Expecting entity callbacks and dirty checking for bulk JPQL.
Forgetting to clear stale managed entities.
interview: Bulk operations trade entity lifecycle behavior for throughput. I use them for large set-based changes and explicitly manage persistence-context consistency.

title: What is the difference between lazy and eager fetching?
short: Lazy fetching defers association loading; eager fetching indicates the association should be available immediately, but neither alone guarantees an optimal SQL query.
answer: Lazy is usually safer for large relationships because data is loaded when needed. However, accessing lazy data outside a valid persistence context can cause LazyInitializationException, while eager mappings can over-fetch. Query-level fetch plans are often preferable.
mistakes: Making everything EAGER to hide LazyInitializationException.
Assuming LAZY means exactly one extra query every time.
interview: Fetch strategy is about when associations become available, not a guarantee about query count. I prefer explicit fetch plans for important read paths.
